cards.front: Supracondylar humerus fracture: commonest elbow fracture in children (FOOSH 5-8y); critical complication is [___] artery injury — always check distal pulses and capillary refill.
cards.context:
Supracondylar humeral fracture is the commonest paediatric elbow fracture — classically 5-8y FOOSH with elbow extended.

Document radial pulse, capillary refill, and AIN function (OK sign) before AND after any manipulation. Untreated forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann's ischaemic contracture (permanent flexion deformity).

cards.front: Holliday-Segar maintenance: first 10 kg = 100 mL/kg/day; second 10 kg = [___] mL/kg/day; each kg after = 20 mL/kg/day.
cards.context:
Daily Holliday-Segar maintenance uses 100/50/20 mL/kg/day for successive weight bands. For 25 kg, this gives 1600 mL/day, or about 67 mL/hour when divided by 24.

The hourly 4-2-1 rule gives 65 mL/hour for the same child. Both are accepted starting estimates, not exact unit conversions.

Adjust for illness and fluid balance; unwell children often need less than full maintenance. Isotonic fluid with glucose is usually preferred.

cards.front: Central precocious puberty in girls is idiopathic in [___] of cases, but in boys an underlying CNS pathology (hypothalamic hamartoma, tumour, hydrocephalus) is present in ~75% — so MRI brain is mandatory in every male.
cards.context:
Central precocious puberty (CPP) is early HPG-axis activation — normal pubertal sequence and progression, but starting too early (girls <8 years, boys <9 years). In girls, >90% is idiopathic.

In boys, 75% have an underlying CNS lesion (hypothalamic hamartoma, tumour, hydrocephalus) — much higher index of suspicion needed. MRI brain is mandatory in boys with CPP.

cards.front: Breast milk jaundice is prolonged [___] jaundice in an otherwise well, thriving breastfed baby.
cards.context:
The picture: a thriving, entirely well breastfed baby who is still visibly yellow beyond the first fortnight, feeding and gaining weight normally, with pigmented stools and pale urine.

The bilirubin is unconjugated and the baby is otherwise normal. It can persist for weeks to a couple of months and then settles without treatment.

cards.front: A child who was walking normally last week now refuses to walk. The weakness is symmetrical and began in the lower limbs, and the pattern is [___].
cards.context: The classic motor pattern starts in the feet and climbs upward over days. A descending pattern points toward botulism or a brainstem cause instead.

cards.front: During an infant's vomiting illness, fewer wet nappies than usual suggest reduced [___] and warrant hydration assessment.
cards.context: RCH recommends assessing urine output relative to normal. Fewer wet nappies are a practical warning to assess feeding and hydration; examine the child rather than diagnose severity from a fixed count.

cards.front: The first-line treatment for anaphylaxis is intramuscular [___] into the anterolateral thigh.
cards.context: One drug, one route, first. IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the immediate treatment — antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, never first-line, and never delay the adrenaline.

cards.front: Absent red reflex (leukocoria) in newborn must rule out retinoblastoma; refer to paediatric ophthalmology [___].
cards.context:
Absent or asymmetric red reflex (LEUKOCORIA — white pupillary reflex) in an infant is a paediatric emergency.

Exam: dim room, ophthalmoscope at arm's length, symmetric red reflex through both pupils — retinoblastoma shows a white reflex in one eye (often noticed on flash photography).

cards.front: Wilms' tumour arises from the kidney; it typically presents at age 1-7 as a large, [___] flank mass with haematuria.
cards.context:
Classically a large, painless flank mass found incidentally by a parent during bathing or dressing in an otherwise well child — the lack of pain is what distinguishes it from an acute abdomen.

Avoid repeated/vigorous abdominal palpation: it risks tumour rupture and intraperitoneal seeding. Good prognosis (~90% survival) with surgery + chemo.

Associated syndromes: WAGR (Wilms, aniridia, genital anomaly, retardation), Beckwith-Wiedemann.

cards.front: Pertussis is most infectious in the [___] phase — before the characteristic cough appears — which is why vulnerable contacts need early prophylactic macrolides.
cards.context:
Pertussis is most transmissible early, in the catarrhal (coryzal) phase, before the paroxysmal whooping cough makes the diagnosis obvious.

This is why prophylactic macrolides for vulnerable contacts (especially unimmunised neonates, in whom pertussis causes apnoea and death) cannot wait for confirmation.

cards.front: IgA vasculitis (HSP): most common childhood vasculitis; triad of palpable purpura (buttocks/lower limbs), arthritis, abdominal pain; monitor for [___].
cards.context:
IgA vasculitis (HSP) is the commonest childhood vasculitis.

Mostly self-limiting; supportive care. Monitor renal function 6-12 months — long-term renal sequelae in 1-2%.

cards.front: RCH defines early-onset neonatal sepsis as onset before [___] hours, but the threshold varies by protocol and should never be presented as universal.
cards.context:
Early- versus late-onset labels are protocol definitions, not universal biological cut-offs. RCH uses under 48 hours for EOS; other protocols use different thresholds.

State the source when quoting a threshold. Clinically, maternal or peripartum acquisition versus community, device or hospital acquisition is what changes the likely pathogens and empiric cover.

cards.front: Otoscopy pinna technique: pull [___]-and-back in adults and older children; pull down-and-back in infants. The infant ear canal is soft and angled differently — adult technique collapses it and you'll see canal wall, not the tympanic membrane.
cards.context:
Pinna manipulation straightens the external auditory canal for line-of-sight to the tympanic membrane.

Wrong technique = looking at canal wall, not the membrane. The infant trap is that adult technique collapses the soft canal.

Use the smallest speculum, brace hand on the child's head, brief glance is enough.

cards.front: After a witnessed choking episode, persistent unilateral wheeze in a toddler is [___] until proven otherwise.
cards.context:
The anatomy (wider, more vertical right main bronchus) only matters once the history has already made aspiration likely.

A witnessed choke followed by persistent unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry is foreign body until bronchoscopy proves otherwise.

cards.front: A well-appearing but febrile infant aged [___] days or younger still needs a full septic screen and empirical IV antibiotics.
cards.context:
A febrile infant aged 28 days or younger by corrected age needs blood, urine and CSF investigation, admission and empiric IV antibiotics even when initially well-appearing.

From 29 days to 3 months the threshold remains low, but investigation, LP, treatment and disposition depend on appearance, focus, results and reliable follow-up rather than a blanket rule for every infant.

cards.front: Raised bilirubin with an unconjugated predominance and otherwise [___] liver enzymes suggests a problem with bilirubin handling, not liver injury.
cards.context:
The pattern to recognise: the bilirubin is up, the unconjugated (indirect) fraction accounts for it, and everything else on the liver panel — the transaminases, ALP and GGT — is normal.

A liver that is genuinely injured or obstructed does not usually leave every other test untouched. So this pattern points either at the handling of bilirubin itself, or at too much bilirubin arriving.

cards.front: A stable 10-month-old with ultrasound-confirmed ileocolic intussusception should undergo [___] reduction first.
cards.context:
Ultrasound confirms ileocolic intussusception with a target sign. In a stable child without perforation or peritonitis, treatment is radiological reduction rather than immediate laparotomy.

Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic; surgery is reserved for instability, perforation or failed enema reduction.

cards.front: The maximum single IM adrenaline dose (1:1000) in anaphylaxis is [___] mg.
cards.context: The 0.01 mg/kg IM dose is capped so heavier children and adolescents are not over-dosed — above roughly 50 kg the weight-based dose reaches this adult ceiling.

cards.front: Children with hand, foot and mouth are admitted for [___], caused by painful oral ulcers stopping oral intake, rather than for the rash itself.
cards.context:
THE ILLNESS IS SELF-LIMITING; THE ADMISSION IS FOR DEHYDRATION. Nobody is admitted because of the rash. They are admitted because the oral ulcers hurt enough that the child stops drinking.

So the management that matters is analgesia and fluid intake — regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, cold fluids, and watching wet nappies and oral intake rather than watching the spots.

Antivirals have no role and antibiotics none. This reframes the whole consultation: the parents are worried about the rash, and the thing you are actually assessing is hydration.

cards.front: Adenotonsillectomy usually [___] paediatric OSA, but residual OSA is common and may require further treatment after reassessment.
cards.context:
Adenotonsillectomy usually improves adenotonsillar OSA but does not guarantee cure.

Residual disease is more likely with severe baseline OSA, obesity, older age, or craniofacial, genetic and neuromuscular comorbidity. Persistent symptoms warrant reassessment; some children need CPAP.

Severe OSA, age under 3, syndromic disease or major comorbidity may require overnight admission. Safety-net for post-tonsillectomy bleeding, including swallowed blood.

cards.front: The drawn-up IM adrenaline dose in paediatric anaphylaxis is [___] mg/kg of 1:1000.
cards.context: When no appropriately-sized auto-injector is available you draw it up: 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 adrenaline. Since 1:1000 = 1 mg/mL, that is 0.01 mL/kg.

cards.front: For most children needing intravenous maintenance without another glucose source, RCH uses sodium chloride 0.9% with [___]% glucose.
cards.context: Glucose forms part of maintenance fluid; this is separate from the fluid bolus used to resuscitate shock.

cards.front: A 6-year-old with two weeks of paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting is PCR-positive for Bordetella pertussis: prescribe a 5-day course of [___].
cards.context:
Confirmation does not change the drug: a PCR-positive child in the paroxysmal phase is still treated — to cut shedding and protect contacts, not to shorten the established cough.

Five days is the whole course — short and well tolerated, which is why it displaced the older 7–14-day erythromycin regimens; the same drug covers post-exposure prophylaxis for household infants.

cards.front: A 12-year-old with exertional breathlessness has FEV1 65% predicted (normal ≥80%), FVC 66% predicted (normal ≥80%) and FEV1/FVC 0.87 (normal ≥0.80). This spirometry pattern is [___].
cards.context:
Read the ratio first. Airway obstruction slows expiration, so FEV1 falls more than FVC and the ratio drops below its lower limit.

Here both volumes fall together and the ratio is preserved: small or stiff lungs, or a chest wall or muscles that cannot expand them.

A low FEV1 on its own is not obstruction. Spirometry only suggests restriction; lung volume testing confirms it.

cards.front: Simple febrile convulsion is generalised, lasts <[___] minutes, occurs in a child within the typical age window for febrile convulsions, has no CNS infection, and does not recur in the same illness.
cards.context:
Simple febrile convulsion has six required features: age 6 months-6 years, generalised tonic-clonic, duration <15 minutes, fever >38°C, no CNS infection, doesn't recur in same febrile illness.

Reassuring; supportive care + identify fever source.

Complex features (focal, prolonged, OR recurrent in same illness) raise later epilepsy risk above the ~1-2% simple-FC baseline: ~6-8% with one feature, ~17-22% with two, ~49% only if all three coexist.

cards.front: For oesophageal food bolus, IV [___] clears the bolus no more often than no therapy at all (~18% vs 17%), while effervescent agents succeed in about 56%.
cards.context:
Glucagon is still widely given on the theory that it relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter, but cohort data show clearance no better than doing nothing, with vomiting as its main contribution.

The cheap fizzy drink beat the drug roughly threefold. Practice lags the evidence here.

cards.front: Congenital hypothyroidism — the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability — is detected on the newborn [___]-prick screen.
cards.context:
The reason it's screened universally: untreated it causes irreversible intellectual disability, but early thyroxine prevents it entirely.

Picked up on the newborn bloodspot (raised TSH), as babies are usually asymptomatic at birth.

cards.front: Breath-holding spells begin in infancy (peak 12-18 months) and typically resolve by age 6 years; trigger → crying → expiratory breath-hold → loss of awareness; benign but check ECG and treat any [___].
cards.context:
Breath-holding spells affect 6 months-6 years (peak 12-18 months, usually resolved by age 6).

Trigger (fear, pain, frustration) → crying → expiratory breath-hold → cyanosis or pallor → stiffening, loss of awareness, sometimes clonic jerks.

Two types: cyanotic (commonest, after crying) and pallid (after pain/fright, vasovagal) — benign, no long-term effects. Iron deficiency association — correction may help; always check ECG to rule out arrhythmia.

cards.front: After treated scarlet fever, antibiotics reduce the later risk of acute [___] fever but do not remove the risk of nephritis.
cards.context:
Treating group A streptococcal pharyngitis prevents acute rheumatic fever if started promptly.

It does not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, so later haematuria still needs assessment.

cards.front: A right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia is easily missed because the [___] plugs the defect, so the film shows an apparently elevated hemidiaphragm rather than the bubbly lucency seen on the left.
cards.context:
Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia is the one that gets missed, and the reason is mechanical.

The liver plugs the defect, so little or no bowel enters the chest and the bubbly lucency that makes the left-sided case obvious never appears.

The film may show only an apparently elevated right hemidiaphragm or a vague basal opacity, and presentation is correspondingly delayed.

cards.front: A child with HSP develops colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. The first-line test to confirm bowel telescoping is [___].
cards.context:
IgA vasculitis can cause bowel-wall oedema and an ileo-ileal intussusception. Colicky pain, vomiting or a palpable mass should not be dismissed as uncomplicated purpura.

Discuss the child with a senior clinician and use ultrasound to confirm intussusception. The location and underlying vasculitis affect the reduction plan.

cards.front: Hand, foot and mouth disease is most commonly caused by [___] A16.
cards.context:
Hand, foot and mouth disease is an enteroviral illness, most often COXSACKIEVIRUS A16. It produces painful oral ulcers together with vesicles on the palms, soles and — very commonly and often forgotten — the buttocks.

It is a clinical diagnosis in a child with a mild fever who looks otherwise well, and it is unrelated to foot-and-mouth disease of livestock, which is a different virus and a question families sometimes ask.

cards.front: Adenotonsillectomy usually improves paediatric OSA, but [___] OSA is common and may require further treatment after reassessment.
cards.context:
Adenotonsillectomy usually improves adenotonsillar OSA but does not guarantee cure.

Residual disease is more likely with severe baseline OSA, obesity, older age, or craniofacial, genetic and neuromuscular comorbidity. Persistent symptoms warrant reassessment; some children need CPAP.

Severe OSA, age under 3, syndromic disease or major comorbidity may require overnight admission. Safety-net for post-tonsillectomy bleeding, including swallowed blood.

cards.front: Six hours after a bicycle crash, a child is hypoxic with increased work of breathing but has no rib fracture and a nearly clear first chest film. The trauma team should suspect pulmonary [___].
cards.context:
The trauma team is reassessing breathing after blunt chest trauma. A compliant paediatric chest wall can transmit force to lung tissue without a rib fracture or striking external bruise.

Hypoxia, respiratory distress or reduced air entry support pulmonary contusion. The first chest film may be normal; radiographic and clinical changes can evolve over the next 24–72 hours, so observation matters.

cards.front: In an infant, subdural haematoma, retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy raise suspicion for abusive head [___], but no finding or triad is diagnostic.
cards.context:
Subdural haematoma, retinal haemorrhage and hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury each increase suspicion for abusive head trauma, especially in infants, but no single finding or triad is diagnostic.

Use a multidisciplinary assessment, examine for other injuries and consider medical and accidental alternatives; an unexplained infant intracranial haemorrhage warrants urgent child-protection evaluation.

cards.front: A child with all three of pallor, easy bruising/bleeding, and recurrent infections has a failing marrow across every cell line (pancytopenia) — the red flag for childhood acute [___].
cards.context:
The single most useful scaffold: leukaemic blasts crowd out the marrow, so all three normal lineages fall at once. Pallor = low red cells, bruising/bleeding = low platelets, infections = low neutrophils.

Any one alone has benign causes; the trap is that the THREE together (a multi-lineage picture) is what points to malignancy rather than to iron deficiency or ordinary viral illness.

cards.front: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers; uses [___] light (450-460 nm); avoid as treatment if primarily conjugated bilirubin is elevated.
cards.context:
Blue light at 450-460 nm converts unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble photoisomers, especially lumirubin, which bypass hepatic conjugation.

Adverse effects: temperature instability, dehydration/loose stools, retinal injury without eye protection, and bronze baby syndrome if conjugated bilirubin is high.

cards.front: High-risk mammal-bite prophylaxis uses [___] to cover Pasteurella and oral anaerobes.
cards.context:
Cat/dog/human bites need thorough washout; antibiotic prophylaxis when indicated is usually amoxicillin–clavulanate (Pasteurella, oral anaerobes, strep/staph).

Duration varies by current protocol: eTG uses 3 days and RCH 5 days; an older Australian Prescriber review described 5–7 days. Follow local AMS rather than treating one duration as universal.

cards.front: A 3-year-old is in asystole with no documented weight. After the APLS weight estimate, the correctly formatted request is 'Adrenaline, 1.4 mL of 1-in-10,000, IV, stat' — a dose of [___] micrograms.
cards.context:
The full chain, done silently before speaking: (3 + 4) x 2 = 14 kg; 14 x 10 microg/kg = 140 microg; at 100 microg/mL that is 1.4 mL.

Asystole is the expected paediatric rhythm, so this dose goes in immediately on access, not after any shock.

If any link is missing — formula, dose, or concentration — the request cannot be formed. That is the point: the format forces the doctor to own the arithmetic.

cards.front: Small inhaled foreign bodies lodge in the bronchial tree, affecting the lower lobes or, on the right, the [___] lobe.
cards.context:
Where the object lodges determines what happens next, and it follows bronchial anatomy.

Only large objects stay in the trachea. Smaller ones reach the bronchial tree and affect the lower lobes, or on the right the middle lobe. Undiagnosed, the child re-presents with pneumonia.

cards.front: Focal inspiratory crackles over a consolidated lung base indicate [___] pathology.
cards.context:
Crackles (crepitations) are discontinuous sounds from opening collapsed alveoli or moving fluid through airspaces — unlike wheeze (narrowed airways) or rhonchi (large-airway secretions).

Focal inspiratory crackles over a consolidated base point to pneumonia, not bronchospasm.

cards.front: Growth velocity is more clinically useful than a single height measurement; crossing [___] centile lines warrants investigation regardless of current percentile.
cards.context:
A single height plotted on a growth chart shows where the child sits vs peers but says little about change.

Crossing 2+ major centile lines (downward = slowing, upward = accelerated) warrants investigation.

Plot serial measurements — frequency 6-monthly under 2y, annually thereafter.

cards.front: Viral-induced wheeze is common in first 2 years; [___] is the dominant trigger in school-aged children.
cards.context:
Respiratory viruses commonly trigger wheeze in young children, who may be well between episodes.

Episodic viral and multi-trigger labels are unreliable preschool subtypes; assess symptoms, episode burden and treatment response over time. Rhinovirus also triggers asthma exacerbations in school-aged children.

Atopy and recurrent wheeze increase concern for persistent asthma, but an infection-only pattern does not exclude it.

cards.front: Mandatory-reporting duties are [___]-specific; a clinician covered by the local law reports when its threshold of reasonable suspicion or belief is met, rather than waiting for proof.
cards.context:
Mandatory-reporting law differs across Australian states and territories: who must report, which maltreatment or harm is reportable, the statutory threshold and the receiving agency all vary.

Apply the law and policy for the relevant jurisdiction. The operative threshold may be reasonable suspicion or reasonable belief and may apply only to specified harm types; proof is not required before acting.

Document exact quotes, injury patterns and caregiver responses. Do not investigate or confront the suspected perpetrator — follow the local child-protection and police pathway.

cards.front: A 3-week-old has sudden green vomiting but looks briefly well between episodes. Until excluded, the surgical diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
Bilious vomiting in a young infant is a surgical emergency because malrotation can twist the mesentery and compromise bowel blood supply.

A briefly well appearance or normal initial radiograph does not safely exclude volvulus.

cards.front: A 5-week-old with a week of cough turns blue and stops breathing during coughing bouts. Between bouts she is afebrile and her chest is clear. The likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
In very young infants the cough can be minimal and the whoop absent, and apnoea or cyanosis may be the only sign.

Bronchiolitis can also cause apnoea at this age, but usually with wheeze or crackles between episodes.

A missing whoop is why this infection is missed in the age group most likely to die of it.

cards.front: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at [___] weeks of age with escalating projectile non-bilious vomiting in a hungry, previously well infant.
cards.context:
An obstructed gastric outlet lets nothing reach the duodenum, so the vomit is forceful, never bile-stained, and the baby is hungry again straight after.

Persistent acid loss drives hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; a firm 'olive' in the right upper quadrant and ultrasound of the pylorus confirm.

cards.front: [___] is the most common congenital infection causing sensorineural hearing loss; can be progressive or late-onset, so needs serial audiological follow-up.
cards.context:
Congenital CMV is the commonest non-genetic cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss — accounts for ~20% of paediatric hearing loss.

Any child with congenital CMV needs serial audiological follow-up through early childhood, even if initial UNHS normal.

cards.front: [___] competence allows a minor to consent to medical treatment if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence; confidentiality has limits (harm to self/others, mandatory reporting).
cards.context:
Gillick competence (UK case law, adopted internationally) lets a minor under 16 consent if they have sufficient understanding to comprehend the proposal — risks, benefits, alternatives.

Confidentiality limits: harm to self/others, mandatory reporting, notifiable diseases.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: FPIES: profuse vomiting [___] hours after ingestion; common triggers include rice, cow's milk, soy.
cards.context:
FPIES is a non-IgE delayed-onset reaction — profuse vomiting 2-4 h after ingestion of trigger food, often with pallor, lethargy, sometimes shock; NO urticaria or other typical allergy features.

Common triggers: rice (paradoxically), cow's milk, soy, oats; skin testing negative; diagnosis clinical. Treatment of acute episode: ondansetron + IV fluids; usually outgrown by 2-4 years.

cards.front: Eighteen hours after blunt chest trauma, a child's pulmonary contusion is producing worsening hypoxia and respiratory distress despite oxygen and analgesia. The trauma team should escalate to [___].
cards.context:
The trauma leader is reviewing a child with a known contusion 18 hours after impact. Worsening hypoxia and respiratory distress indicate evolving lung haemorrhage and oedema, not reassurance from an earlier film.

Give oxygen and analgesia while monitoring saturation and work of breathing. If gas exchange or effort worsens despite those measures, escalate to ventilatory support; the level depends on severity.

cards.front: Positive skin prick test alone does NOT diagnose allergy — it shows sensitisation; wheal size indicates [___], not severity of reaction.
cards.context: Sensitisation (positive SPT or specific IgE) means the immune system has produced IgE against an allergen — but doesn't prove clinical allergy. ~10% of children are sensitised to peanut on testing.

cards.front: A brisk LH rise after a GnRH challenge classifies precocious puberty as [___] (HPG-axis driven).
cards.context:
Central precocious puberty is HPG-axis activation — the hypothalamus has woken up early and is pulsing GnRH, so the pituitary responds briskly to a GnRH challenge with an LH rise.

Peripheral (gonadotrophin-independent) causes do not, because the axis isn't driving it. Central precocity is then treated with a GnRH analogue that desensitises the pituitary.

A peripheral source must instead be hunted down: CAH, McCune-Albright, or a gonadal or adrenal tumour.

cards.front: At 19 months, a boy's left testis lies in the groin and can be eased down only to the top of the scrotum, under tension. His mother asks about waiting a year. The GP's plan now is [___].
cards.context:
A retractile testis reaches the base of the scrotum without tension and needs only review. One that stops short under tension is undescended.

A testis still undescended after the first 3 months is unlikely to come down on its own, so waiting at 19 months achieves nothing.

Surgery is advised between 6 and 12 months to protect fertility and may lower cancer risk. This boy is already past that window, so the referral is made now.

cards.front: Homemade ORS: 1 L water + 6 tsp sugar + ½ tsp [___].
cards.context: Prefer commercial low-osmolarity ORS. Homemade fallback: 1 L clean water + 6 tsp sugar + ½ tsp salt — enough glucose for SGLT without a lethal salt load.

cards.front: Hyperinflation in cystic fibrosis narrows the cardiac outline, so an enlarged cardiac silhouette should raise suspicion of heart failure or [___].
cards.context:
Cor pulmonale is right-ventricular enlargement, with possible failure, caused by pulmonary hypertension from lung disease.

In advanced cystic fibrosis, chronic hypoxia and lung damage raise pulmonary vascular resistance. The right ventricle works against this increased pressure.

Hyperinflation usually narrows the cardiac silhouette. Enlargement therefore warrants assessment; a chest radiograph alone cannot diagnose cor pulmonale.

cards.front: Before sending home a well 9-week-old after a single 20-second BRUE, the ED doctor checks the low-risk criteria, including birth at or after [___] weeks' gestation.
cards.context:
Low risk also needs nothing concerning on history or exam, age over 60 days, corrected gestational age of 45 weeks or more, a first event under 1 minute, and no CPR by a trained provider.

Infants born before 32 weeks have immature control of breathing, which is why gestation is a criterion. Failing any one criterion makes it a higher-risk BRUE.

A low-risk BRUE needs no investigations. The infant can go home if parents feel reassured, with clear return advice and an offer of infant CPR training.

cards.front: [___]-hydroxylase deficiency causes 95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH); autosomal recessive; newborn screen detects elevated 17-OHP.
cards.context:
21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for ~95% of CAH cases. Autosomal recessive.

The enzyme block prevents cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, shunting precursors to androgens (causing virilisation in females, salt-wasting from aldosterone deficiency).

cards.front: Inhaled corticosteroids act on an intracellular receptor to alter gene [___], which is why the benefit takes weeks rather than minutes.
cards.context:
ICS act through the intracellular glucocorticoid receptor; the complex moves to the nucleus and changes gene transcription.

Anti-inflammatory genes are transactivated and pro-inflammatory factors such as NF-kappa-B and AP-1 transrepressed, leaving fewer eosinophils, mast cells and activated T cells in the airway wall.

Because it works through transcription it takes days to weeks — so a preventer does nothing for an acute attack and must be taken daily when well.
